title: Geometry — Shapes & Area
blurb: Angles and their sums, triangles and the quadrilateral family, perimeter as the boundary walk, area as the tile count, and composite figures solved down two agreeing roads.

lessons.title: Angles
lessons.concreteComparison: A ger door swings from closed to wide open — and how far it swung is an ANGLE: an amount of turn. The corner of this page turns a quarter of a full spin; we call that a right angle and give it $90$ degrees. Every other angle is measured against it: less than the corner is acute, more is obtuse, and half a full spin — the flat line — is $180^\circ$.
lessons.objective: Measure and classify angles in degrees against the right-angle benchmark, and find missing angles on a straight line and around a point.
concept: **An angle is turn, not length.** Degrees count how far something turned: a full spin is $360^\circ$, half a spin (a straight line) $180^\circ$, a quarter (the page's corner) $90^\circ$ — the RIGHT angle, geometry's benchmark.

**Classify against the benchmark.** Acute: less than $90^\circ$ (a sharp wedge). Obtuse: between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ (a lazy recliner). The arms' LENGTH never matters — a tiny drawn angle of $120^\circ$ still beats a huge drawn one of $45^\circ$.

**The two great sums.** Angles that fill a straight line total $180^\circ$; angles that fill a full turn total $360^\circ$. Both work as subtraction machines: a missing angle is the total minus the known ones — $180 - 65 = 115$.
lessons.keyIdea: An angle measures turn, judged against the 90-degree right angle; straight lines carry 180 degrees and full turns 360, and missing angles fall out by subtraction.

facts.title: The benchmarks
facts.explanation: Quarter, half, and whole of one spin — everything is measured against these.

facts.title: The subtraction machines
facts.explanation: Missing angles are totals minus the angles you can see.

workedExamples.statement: Two angles share a straight line; one measures $65^\circ$. Find the other, and classify both.
workedExamples.solution: $180 - 65 = 115^\circ$. The $65^\circ$ angle is acute (under $90$); the $115^\circ$ angle is obtuse (between $90$ and $180$). Check: $65 + 115 = 180$ ✓.

workedExamples.statement: Three angles meet around a point: $140^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and one unknown. Find it.

commonMistakes.text: Judging an angle by the length of its drawn arms.
commonMistakes.correction: The arms are just rays — only the TURN between them counts. A 120° angle drawn small still beats a 45° angle drawn across the page.

commonMistakes.text: Using 360 for a straight line (or 180 for a full turn).
commonMistakes.correction: A straight line is HALF a spin: 180°. Ask 'line or full turn?' before subtracting — the wrong total doubles or halves every answer.

tryIt.statement: On a straight line, two equal angles sit side by side. How big is each?
tryIt.solution: They share $180^\circ$ equally: $180 \div 2 = 90^\circ$ each — two right angles, which is exactly what a perpendicular crossing makes.

steps.title: Turn, measured in degrees
beats: An angle is an amount of TURN — the ger door swinging open, the clock hand sweeping. Degrees count the turn: a full spin is $360^\circ$.
The benchmarks: quarter spin $= 90^\circ$ (the RIGHT angle — the page's corner), half spin $= 180^\circ$ (a straight line).
Classify against them: acute $< 90^\circ$, obtuse between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Arm length is irrelevant — only the turn counts.

steps.title: Naming turns
steps.intro: Compare with 90 and 180; the arms' length never votes.

examples.prompt: Classify $38^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $155^\circ$, $180^\circ$.
Which is bigger: a $120^\circ$ angle drawn with short arms, or a $45^\circ$ angle drawn with long arms?
steps: The short-armed angle wins — drawing size is a costume.

problems.prompt: An angle of $89^\circ$ is:
problems.explanation: One degree under the benchmark — still acute. Classification is exact, not approximate.

problems.prompt: A clock's hands at 3:00 make an angle of:
problems.explanation: Quarter of the face — a right angle. (The full face is $360^\circ$; each hour mark is $30^\circ$, and three of them make $90$.)

problems.prompt: Half of a right angle measures:
problems.explanation: $90 \div 2 = 45^\circ$ — the diagonal-fold angle.

steps.title: Costume check
steps.prompt: Two angles are drawn: one tiny with $130^\circ$ of turn, one huge with $70^\circ$. The bigger ANGLE is:
steps.explanation: Angles measure turn, not ink: $130 > 70$, whatever the arm lengths. The drawing's size is a costume the angle wears.

steps.title: Why 360?
steps.body: The Babylonians again (time's sixty-traders): $360$ divides cleanly by $2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12$ and more — so halves, thirds, quarters and fifths of a turn all come out whole. A decimal circle of $100^\circ$ would make a third of a turn $33.33\ldots$ — forever.

steps.title: The two great sums
beats: Angles filling a STRAIGHT LINE total $180^\circ$ — so a missing one is $180$ minus the known: $180 - 65 = 115^\circ$.
Angles filling a FULL TURN total $360^\circ$: $360 - 140 - 90 = 130^\circ$.
Ask 'line or turn?' before subtracting — the totals are the whole method, and picking the wrong one doubles or halves everything.

examples.prompt: Two angles on a line; one is $65^\circ$. The other?
Around a point: $140^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and one unknown.

problems.prompt: On a straight line, next to a $48^\circ$ angle:
problems.explanation: $180 - 48 = 132^\circ$. ($312$ used the full-turn total on a line.)

problems.prompt: Around a point sit $100^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $85^\circ$ and one more:
Two equal angles fill a straight line. Each is:
problems.explanation: $180 \div 2 = 90$ — a perpendicular crossing.

steps.title: Line or turn?
steps.prompt: Four equal angles meet around a point. Each measures:
steps.explanation: The point carries $360$: $360 \div 4 = 90^\circ$ — four right angles, like the corners meeting at a window's cross-frame.

steps.title: What you learned
points: An angle measures TURN in degrees; arm length never votes.
Benchmarks: right 90°, straight 180°, full turn 360°.
Acute is under 90; obtuse sits between 90 and 180.
Missing angles: total (180 on a line, 360 at a point) minus the known.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every missing angle, first say which total applies — 'line, 180' or 'point, 360' — then subtract. The naming is the method.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Classifying and the two sums together.

problems.prompt: An angle of $91^\circ$ is:
problems.explanation: One degree past the benchmark — obtuse. Exact boundaries, no rounding.

problems.prompt: On a line beside a right angle sits:
problems.explanation: $180 - 90 = 90^\circ$ — right angles come in pairs on a line.

problems.prompt: A pizza is cut into $8$ equal slices. Each slice's tip angle is:
problems.explanation: $360 \div 8 = 45^\circ$ per slice.

problems.prompt: Around a point, three angles are $150^\circ$, $150^\circ$, and:
The hands of a clock at 6:00 form:
problems.explanation: Opposite directions along one line: half a spin, $180^\circ$ ($6 \times 30$).

steps.title: You've finished "Angles"
steps.body: Turn, benchmarks, and two subtraction machines. Next: the shapes those angles build — triangles and quadrilaterals, each carrying a fixed angle budget.

lessons.title: Triangles & Quadrilaterals
lessons.concreteComparison: Tear the three corners off ANY paper triangle and lay them side by side: they always build a straight line — $180^\circ$, every triangle, every time. Shapes carry fixed angle budgets: triangles get $180^\circ$ to share among three corners, quadrilaterals get $360^\circ$ among four. Classifying shapes is reading how they spend it.
lessons.objective: Classify triangles by sides and by angles, know the quadrilateral family, and use the angle budgets — 180 for triangles, 360 for quadrilaterals — to find missing angles.
concept: **Triangles, by sides and by angles.** Sides: equilateral (all three equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (none). Angles: right (one $90^\circ$), acute (all under $90$), obtuse (one over). Every triangle earns one name from each list.

**The 180 budget.** A triangle's three angles always total $180^\circ$ — so the third is $180$ minus the two known: $180 - 90 - 35 = 55^\circ$. An equilateral triangle splits the budget evenly: $60^\circ$ each.

**The quadrilateral family and its 360.** Squares are special rectangles; rectangles and rhombuses are special parallelograms; a trapezoid has just one parallel pair. All of them spend exactly $360^\circ$: $360 - 90 - 90 - 110 = 70^\circ$.
lessons.keyIdea: Shapes carry fixed angle budgets — 180 degrees for triangles, 360 for quadrilaterals — and their names describe how sides and angles spend it.

facts.title: The budgets
facts.explanation: Three corners share 180; four corners share 360 — always.

facts.title: The family tree
facts.explanation: Every square is a rectangle; every rectangle is a parallelogram — special cases nest.

workedExamples.statement: A right triangle has one angle of $35^\circ$. Find the third angle and classify the triangle by its angles.
workedExamples.solution: $180 - 90 - 35 = 55^\circ$. One angle is exactly $90^\circ$, so it is a RIGHT triangle (the other two, $35^\circ$ and $55^\circ$, are both acute — as they must be, since only $90$ remains for them together).

workedExamples.statement: A quadrilateral has angles $90^\circ$, $90^\circ$ and $110^\circ$. Find the fourth.
workedExamples.solution: $360 - 90 - 90 - 110 = 70^\circ$. Check: $90 + 90 + 110 + 70 = 360$ ✓. (Two right angles but not four — so this is not a rectangle.)

commonMistakes.text: Refusing to call a square a rectangle.
commonMistakes.correction: A rectangle needs four right angles — a square has them (plus equal sides as a bonus). Special cases BELONG to the family: every square is a rectangle, every rectangle a parallelogram.

commonMistakes.text: Using the 360 budget on a triangle.
commonMistakes.correction: Three corners share 180, four share 360. Count the corners before subtracting — the wrong budget makes angles that cannot close.

tryIt.statement: A triangle has angles $70^\circ$ and $70^\circ$. Find the third, and classify by sides and by angles.
tryIt.solution: $180 - 70 - 70 = 40^\circ$. Two equal angles mean two equal sides: isosceles; and all angles under $90$: acute.

tryIt.statement: Every angle of an equilateral triangle measures the same. How big is each?
tryIt.solution: The budget splits three ways: $180 \div 3 = 60^\circ$ each.

steps.title: Triangles and their 180
beats: Tear the corners off any paper triangle and line them up: a straight line — $180^\circ$, always. That's the triangle's angle budget.
Missing angles fall out by subtraction: a right triangle with a $35^\circ$ corner keeps $180 - 90 - 35 = 55^\circ$ for the third.
Names: by sides — equilateral (three equal), isosceles (two), scalene (none); by angles — right, acute, obtuse. Every triangle gets one of each.

examples.prompt: A right triangle has a $35^\circ$ angle. The third?
steps: The two non-right corners always share exactly $90$: here $35 + 55$ ✓.

examples.prompt: An isosceles triangle has two $70^\circ$ angles. The third — and the full classification?
steps: Isosceles (two equal sides) and acute (all corners under $90$).

problems.prompt: A triangle has angles $25^\circ$ and $115^\circ$. The third is:
problems.explanation: $180 - 25 - 115 = 40^\circ$ — and the $115$ makes it an obtuse triangle.

problems.prompt: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is:
problems.explanation: $180 \div 3 = 60^\circ$ — the budget shared perfectly evenly.

problems.prompt: Can a triangle have TWO right angles?
options: no — they alone would spend the whole $180$, leaving nothing
problems.explanation: $90 + 90 = 180$ uses the entire budget before the third corner exists. One right angle is the maximum.

steps.title: Read the sides
steps.prompt: A triangle with sides $7$, $7$ and $4$ cm is:
steps.explanation: Two sevens and a four: isosceles. (Side names and angle names are separate — this one could be acute or obtuse; the sides alone can't say.)

steps.title: The torn-corners proof
steps.body: The corner-tearing trick isn't just a demonstration — it IS the idea behind the real proof: the three angles reassemble along a straight line through the top vertex. You can do honest mathematics with a piece of paper and torn corners.

steps.title: The quadrilateral family
beats: Four sides, four corners, $360^\circ$ to spend. Missing angles: $360$ minus the rest — $360 - 90 - 90 - 110 = 70^\circ$.

The family nests: a PARALLELOGRAM has two parallel pairs; make its angles right and it's a RECTANGLE; make a rectangle's sides equal and it's a SQUARE. A RHOMBUS is a parallelogram with equal sides; a TRAPEZOID has just one parallel pair.
Nesting means membership: every square IS a rectangle and IS a parallelogram — special cases don't leave the family, they lead it.

examples.prompt: Angles $90^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $110^\circ$ — the fourth?
steps: Not a rectangle: only two of the four corners are right.

examples.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle of $65^\circ$. Its neighbour angle?
steps: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram sit on a line of parallels: they total $180$.

problems.prompt: A quadrilateral has angles $80^\circ$, $100^\circ$, $95^\circ$ and:
Which statement is TRUE?
problems.explanation: A square has four right angles — a rectangle's only requirement. The reverse fails: rectangles needn't have equal sides.

problems.prompt: A shape with exactly ONE pair of parallel sides is a:
problems.explanation: One pair: trapezoid. (Two pairs makes the parallelogram family.)

steps.title: The nested names
steps.prompt: A rhombus with four right angles is also called:
steps.explanation: Equal sides (rhombus) + right angles (rectangle) = square — the shape at the top of the family tree wears every name below it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Triangle budget: 180°; quadrilateral budget: 360° — count corners first.
Triangles take one name by sides (equilateral/isosceles/scalene) and one by angles (right/acute/obtuse).
The family nests: square ⊂ rectangle ⊂ parallelogram; rhombus joins at the parallelogram level; trapezoid keeps one parallel pair.
Two right angles use a triangle's whole budget — so at most one per triangle.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each shape, name the budget aloud before subtracting — and for each family question, ask what the shape's requirements are, not what it looks like.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Budgets, names, and the family tree.

problems.prompt: A triangle has a $102^\circ$ angle and a $39^\circ$ angle. The third:
problems.explanation: $180 - 102 - 39 = 39^\circ$: two equal angles — isosceles, and obtuse thanks to the $102$.

problems.prompt: Which triangle CANNOT exist?
problems.explanation: $90 + 50 + 50 = 190 \ne 180$ — the budget doesn't close. The others total $180$ exactly.

problems.prompt: A rectangle's four angles total:
problems.explanation: Four right angles: $4 \times 90 = 360$ — the quadrilateral budget, spent entirely on corners.

problems.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle of $70^\circ$. Its four angles are:
problems.explanation: Opposites repeat, neighbours complete $180$: $70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360$ ✓.

problems.prompt: True or false: some trapezoids are parallelograms.
options: false — one parallel pair, by definition, is not two
problems.explanation: A trapezoid's defining feature is exactly ONE parallel pair; a parallelogram needs two. The definitions part ways.

steps.title: You've finished "Triangles & Quadrilaterals"
steps.body: Angle budgets and a family tree — the naming half of geometry. Next: measuring the shapes themselves, starting with the walk around the edge.

lessons.title: Perimeter
lessons.concreteComparison: A herder fencing a rectangular paddock $8$ m by $5$ m doesn't need to guess the wire: walk the boundary — $8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26$ m. Perimeter is exactly that walk, and the rectangle's shortcut $2 \times (8 + 5)$ is just the walk noticing that opposite sides match.
lessons.objective: Find perimeters of rectangles, squares and composite shapes by walking the boundary, use the rectangle shortcut, and work backwards to a missing side.
concept: **Perimeter is the walk around.** Add EVERY side once — the fence's length, the frame's wood. Units are linear: metres, centimetres.
**Rectangles shortcut it.** Opposite sides match, so $P = 2 \times (l + w)$: the $8 \times 5$ paddock takes $2 \times 13 = 26$ m. Squares compress further: $P = 4s$.

**Backwards to a missing side.** Know $P = 30$ and $l = 9$? Halve first — $l + w = 15$ — then $w = 15 - 9 = 6$. And on composite (L-shaped) walks, count EVERY edge, notches included: the walk doesn't skip the dent.
lessons.keyIdea: Perimeter walks the whole boundary once — rectangles shortcut it as twice length-plus-width, and missing sides come from running the shortcut backwards.

facts.title: The shortcuts
facts.explanation: Opposite sides match; the walk folds in half (or quarters).

facts.title: Backwards
facts.explanation: Halve the perimeter to get one length-plus-width; subtract the known side.

workedExamples.statement: Find the perimeter of an $8$ m by $5$ m paddock, and of a square pen with $7$ m sides.
workedExamples.solution: Paddock: $8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26$ m — or the shortcut, $2 \times (8 + 5) = 26$ m. Square pen: $4 \times 7 = 28$ m.

workedExamples.statement: A rectangle has perimeter $30$ cm and length $9$ cm. Find its width.
workedExamples.solution: Half the walk covers one length and one width: $30 \div 2 = 15$, so $w = 15 - 9 = 6$ cm. Check: $2 \times (9 + 6) = 30$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Adding only the two labelled sides — P of an 8 × 5 rectangle as 13.
commonMistakes.correction: The walk passes FOUR sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5. The shortcut 2(l + w) has the ×2 precisely because labels show only half the boundary.

commonMistakes.text: Forgetting to halve when working backwards — w = 30 − 9 = 21.
commonMistakes.correction: P covers TWO lengths and TWO widths. Halve first (l + w = 15), then subtract: w = 6. A 21-wide rectangle would need P = 60.

tryIt.statement: A photo frame is $24$ cm by $18$ cm. How much wooden edging does it need?
A square garden takes $36$ m of fence. How long is each side?

steps.title: Walk the boundary
beats: Perimeter is the walk around the edge — every side once, in linear units (m, cm).
Rectangles shortcut the walk: opposite sides match, so $P = 2(l + w)$ — the $8 \times 5$ paddock takes $2 \times 13 = 26$ m of fence.
Squares compress it further: four equal sides, $P = 4s$.

examples.prompt: Perimeter of an $8 \times 5$ paddock and a $7$ m square pen.
Edging for a $24 \times 18$ cm frame.

steps.title: Boundary walks
steps.intro: Every side once; shortcut when sides repeat.

problems.prompt: A $12 \times 7$ m garden's perimeter is:
problems.explanation: $2(12 + 7) = 38$ m. ($19$ walked only half; $84$ multiplied — that's the area's business.)

problems.prompt: A square tile of side $15$ cm has perimeter:
problems.explanation: $4 \times 15 = 60$ cm. ($225$ is the area again, sneaking in.)

problems.prompt: A triangle with sides $9$, $12$ and $15$ cm has perimeter:
problems.explanation: No shortcut for scalene sides — walk all three: $9 + 12 + 15 = 36$ cm.

steps.title: Half a walk
steps.prompt: A student finds the perimeter of an $8 \times 5$ rectangle as $8 + 5 = 13$. The slip:
options: only half the boundary was walked — four sides make $26$
steps.explanation: The label shows one length and one width, but the walk passes TWO of each: $2 \times 13 = 26$. The shortcut's $\times 2$ exists exactly for this.

steps.title: The fence-post problem
steps.body: Fencing a $26$ m perimeter with posts every metre needs exactly $26$ posts, not $27$ — on a CLOSED loop the last post is the first one. On a straight $26$ m fence you'd need $27$. Boundary problems care whether the walk comes home.

steps.title: Backwards, and around the notch
beats: Missing sides run the shortcut backwards: $P = 30$, $l = 9$ — halve first ($l + w = 15$), then $w = 6$.
Squares: $P = 36$ gives $s = 9$ in one division.
Composite shapes have no shortcut — walk EVERY edge, notches included. An L-shaped walk turns six corners, and each little edge counts.

steps.title: Running it backwards
steps.intro: Halve, subtract; or divide by four.

examples.prompt: $P = 30$ cm, length $9$ cm — the width?
A square garden takes $36$ m of fence. Each side?

steps.title: Missing pieces
steps.intro: Halve for rectangles; quarter for squares.

problems.prompt: $P = 44$ m, width $8$ m. The length is:
A square with perimeter $52$ cm has sides of:
An L-shaped path has six edges: $10, 4, 6, 3, 4, 7$ m. Its perimeter is:
problems.explanation: Walk them all: $10 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 4 + 7 = 34$ m — the notch's little edges count too.

steps.title: The forgotten halving
steps.prompt: $P = 40$ and $l = 12$: a student writes $w = 40 - 12 = 28$. The check $2(12 + 28)$ gives:
options: $80$ — twice the stated perimeter, so the halving was skipped
steps.explanation: $2 \times 40 = 80 \ne 40$: the receipt fails. Halve first: $l + w = 20$, so $w = 8$ (and $2 \times 20 = 40$ ✓).

steps.title: What you learned
points: Perimeter walks every side once — linear units.
Rectangle shortcut: 2(l + w); square: 4s.
Backwards: halve the perimeter, then subtract the known side.
Composite shapes: no shortcut — walk every edge, notches included.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Receipt every backwards answer by rebuilding the perimeter — the forgotten halving fails its receipt instantly.

problems.prompt: A $30 \times 20$ m yard needs how much fencing?
problems.explanation: $2(30 + 20) = 100$ m. ($600$ is the area trying to buy fence.)

problems.prompt: An equilateral triangle of side $14$ cm has perimeter:
problems.explanation: $3 \times 14 = 42$ cm.

problems.prompt: $P = 50$ cm and the length is $15$ cm. The width:
A running track goes around a $90 \times 60$ m field. Four laps cover:
Which rectangle does NOT have perimeter $24$?

steps.title: You've finished "Perimeter"
steps.body: The boundary is measured; next we count what's INSIDE it — and discover that two rectangles with the same fence can hold very different fields.

lessons.title: Area of Rectangles
lessons.concreteComparison: Tiling a floor with $1$-metre-square carpet tiles: an $8 \times 5$ room takes $8$ tiles per row, $5$ rows — $40$ tiles. AREA is that count of unit squares, and $l \times w$ is just rows-times-row-length: multiplication's array picture laid on the floor.
lessons.objective: Find areas of rectangles and squares in square units, keep area's units distinct from perimeter's, work back to a missing side, and see that equal perimeters can hold different areas.
concept: **Area counts unit squares.** An $8 \times 5$ m room holds $8 \times 5 = 40$ one-metre squares: $40$ m². The formula IS the tiling — rows times row-length.

**Square units, not linear ones.** Perimeter answers in m (a length of fence); area answers in m² (a count of tiles). Writing $40$ m for an area is the units trap — the little $^2$ records that tiles are squares.

**Same fence, different fields.** $6 \times 4$ and $8 \times 2$ both take $20$ m of fence — but hold $24$ m² and $16$ m². Perimeter does not determine area; among rectangles with equal perimeter, the SQUARE holds the most.
lessons.keyIdea: Area is the count of unit squares — length times width, answered in square units — and rectangles sharing a perimeter can hold very different areas.

facts.title: The tiling formula
facts.explanation: Rows times row-length — multiplication's array on the floor.

facts.title: Same fence, different fields
facts.explanation: Equal perimeters, unequal areas — the squarer shape holds more.

workedExamples.statement: A room is $8$ m by $5$ m. How many $1$ m² carpet tiles cover it — and what are the room's area and perimeter, with correct units?
workedExamples.note: Keep the two measures side by side.
workedExamples.solution: Tiles: $8$ per row, $5$ rows — $8 \times 5 = 40$ tiles, so the area is $40$ m². The perimeter is $2(8 + 5) = 26$ m — metres of skirting board, not tiles. Two different questions, two different units.

workedExamples.statement: Compare the $6 \times 4$ and $8 \times 2$ rectangles: perimeter and area of each.
workedExamples.solution: Perimeters: $2(6+4) = 20$ and $2(8+2) = 20$ — identical fences. Areas: $24$ m² against $16$ m² — the squarer shape holds $8$ m² more. Perimeter does not decide area.

commonMistakes.text: Answering area in linear units — "the area is 40 m".
commonMistakes.correction: Area counts SQUARES: 40 m². The exponent isn't decoration — it says what kind of thing was counted (tiles, not fence).

commonMistakes.text: Assuming equal perimeters mean equal areas.
commonMistakes.correction: 6 × 4 and 8 × 2 share a 20 m fence but hold 24 and 16 m². Fence length constrains, it doesn't determine — the squarer rectangle always holds more.

tryIt.statement: A courtyard is $12$ m by $9$ m. Find its area and its perimeter, with units.
A rectangle has area $72$ cm² and length $9$ cm. Find its width.

steps.title: Count the tiles
beats: Cover a floor with $1$-metre squares: $8$ per row, $5$ rows — $40$ tiles. AREA is that count: $A = l \times w = 40$ m².
The unit is a SQUARE metre — a tile one metre on each side. The little $^2$ records what was counted.
Squares tile as $s \times s = s^2$: a $15$ cm square tile covers $225$ cm².

examples.prompt: Area and perimeter of an $8 \times 5$ m room.
steps: Perimeter: $2(8+5) = 26$ m — skirting board. Different questions, different units.

examples.prompt: Area of a $12 \times 9$ m courtyard.

problems.prompt: A $7 \times 6$ m floor has area:
problems.explanation: $7 \times 6 = 42$ — square metres, because tiles were counted. ($26$ m is the perimeter crashing the party; $42$ m wears the wrong unit.)

problems.prompt: A square window of side $9$ dm has area:
problems.explanation: $9^2 = 81$ dm². ($36$ is its perimeter.)

problems.prompt: A rectangle of area $72$ cm² and length $9$ cm has width:
problems.explanation: $72 \div 9 = 8$; receipt $9 \times 8 = 72$ ✓ — division undoes the tiling.

steps.title: The units trap
steps.prompt: "The garden's area is $54$ m" — what's wrong?
options: areas count squares: it should be $54$ m²
steps.explanation: $54$ METRES is a length — a fence, a walk. The garden's inside was counted in square-metre tiles: $54$ m². The exponent is the receipt for WHAT was counted.

steps.title: A hectare is a square you can see
steps.body: Land is measured in hectares: one hectare is a $100 \times 100$ m square — $10\,000$ m², about a large sports field. A herder family's winter pasture might span hundreds of them.

steps.title: Same fence, different fields
beats: Two rectangles can share a fence and disagree about their fields: $6 \times 4$ and $8 \times 2$ both take $20$ m — but hold $24$ m² and $16$ m².
Stretch a rectangle thinner at fixed perimeter and its area DRAINS: $9 \times 1$ holds just $9$ m² of the same $20$ m fence.
Among equal-perimeter rectangles the SQUARE holds the most: $5 \times 5 = 25$ m² tops them all. Fence constrains; shape decides.

examples.prompt: Compare $6 \times 4$ and $8 \times 2$ on a $20$ m fence.
steps: The squarer shape holds $8$ m² more.

examples.prompt: Best rectangle on that same fence?
steps: The square — always the biggest field for the fence.

steps.title: Fence economics
steps.intro: Fix the perimeter; watch the area move.

problems.prompt: Which holds MORE on a $24$ m fence: $8 \times 4$ or $10 \times 2$?
problems.explanation: Both walk $24$ m; the fields differ: $32$ vs $20$ m².

problems.prompt: The BIGGEST rectangular field a $24$ m fence can hold is:
problems.explanation: The square again: $2(6+6) = 24$ and $36$ m² — more than any longer-thinner cousin.

problems.prompt: Two rectangles have the same AREA of $36$ cm²: $6 \times 6$ and $12 \times 3$. Their perimeters:
problems.explanation: Same field, different fences: the thin one walks farther. (The coin has two sides.)

steps.title: Fence vs field
steps.prompt: A farmer with $40$ m of fence wants the biggest rectangular plot. She should build:
steps.explanation: All three use the $40$ m fence, but the square's field crushes the strip's: $100$ vs $36$ m². Squareness pays.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Area = count of unit squares = l × w, answered in square units.
Perimeter is fence (m); area is tiles (m²) — the exponent is the receipt.
Missing side: divide the area by the known side.
Equal fences can hold unequal fields; the square holds the most.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Write the unit BEFORE computing each answer — deciding 'm or m²?' first makes the fence/field confusion impossible.

problems.prompt: A $15 \times 4$ m corridor has area:
problems.explanation: $15 \times 4 = 60$ m². ($38$ m is its perimeter.)

problems.prompt: A square field of area $49$ m² has sides of:
problems.explanation: $7 \times 7 = 49$: seven metres.

problems.prompt: Compare a $9 \times 4$ board and an $8 \times 5$ board. Which statement is true?
options: the two boards have equal areas
$8 \times 5$ has more area for the same perimeter
problems.explanation: Areas: $36$ vs $40$ — $8 \times 5$ paints more. Perimeters: $26$ vs $26$ — equal tape! Same fence, different fields, live on a workbench.

problems.prompt: A room of $5 \times 4$ m is carpeted with $1$ m² tiles costing $8\,000$ tögrög each. The carpet costs:
Doubling BOTH sides of a $6 \times 3$ rectangle multiplies its area by:
problems.explanation: $6 \times 3 = 18$; doubled, $12 \times 6 = 72 = 4 \times 18$. Two doublings compound — one per direction.

steps.title: You've finished "Area of Rectangles"
steps.body: Tiles counted, units disciplined, and the fence/field distinction earned. Finale: shapes made of several rectangles — where two different roads must meet at one answer.

lessons.title: Composite Areas
lessons.concreteComparison: An L-shaped room — a rectangle with a corner bitten out — has no single formula. But two roads reach its area: CUT it into two rectangles and add, or take the FULL rectangle and subtract the bite. Both roads must land on the same number; when they do, you've proof-read your own answer.
lessons.objective: Find areas of L-shaped and composite rectilinear figures by splitting into rectangles or subtracting the missing piece, recover unlabelled side lengths, and keep composite area and perimeter separate.
concept: **Road one: split and add.** Cut the L into two rectangles, area each, add. An $8 \times 6$ room with a $3 \times 2$ corner bite splits into $8 \times 4$ and $5 \times 2$: $32 + 10 = 42$ m².
**Road two: fill and subtract.** Restore the full $8 \times 6$ rectangle ($48$ m²), subtract the bite ($3 \times 2 = 6$): $48 - 6 = 42$ m². Two roads, one answer — and the agreement is your receipt.
**Unlabelled sides come from the labels.** Opposite spans must match: if the top edge is $8$ and one lower piece is $3$, the other is $8 - 3 = 5$. Every missing edge is a difference of labelled ones.
lessons.keyIdea: Composite areas travel two roads — split-and-add or fill-and-subtract — and the roads must agree; missing edges are differences of the labelled ones.

facts.title: Two roads
facts.explanation: Add the pieces, or remove the bite — agreement is the receipt.

facts.title: Missing edges
facts.explanation: Opposite spans match; unlabelled sides are differences of labelled ones.

workedExamples.statement: An L-shaped room is an $8 \times 6$ m rectangle with a $3 \times 2$ m bite out of one corner. Find its area by BOTH roads.
workedExamples.solution: Split: a full-width $8 \times 4$ strip ($32$) plus the remaining $5 \times 2$ strip ($10$ — its width is $8 - 3 = 5$): $42$ m². Subtract: $8 \times 6 = 48$ minus the $3 \times 2 = 6$ bite: $42$ m². The roads agree — that's the receipt.

workedExamples.statement: A T-shaped stage is a $10 \times 3$ m bar on top of a $4 \times 5$ m stem. Find its area, and note which road you used.
workedExamples.note: This one splits naturally — there's no simple surrounding rectangle.
workedExamples.solution: Split: bar $10 \times 3 = 30$; stem $4 \times 5 = 20$; total $50$ m². (Fill-and-subtract works too but needs a $10 \times 8$ surround minus two $3 \times 5$ shoulders: $80 - 30 = 50$ — same answer, longer road.)

commonMistakes.text: Multiplying the two biggest labels — the L-shape as 8 × 6 = 48.
commonMistakes.correction: 48 is the FULL rectangle; the bite must leave. Either subtract it (48 − 6) or split honestly — the L holds 42.
The cut pieces must not overlap: an 8 × 4 strip plus a 5 × 2 strip tile the L exactly. If your pieces share squares, the sum overshoots.

tryIt.statement: A $9 \times 7$ m yard has a $4 \times 3$ m shed in one corner. How much OPEN yard remains?
An L-shape's top edge is $12$ m; the lower-right piece's top is $7$ m. How long is the unlabelled upper-left span?

steps.title: Two roads to one answer
beats: An L-shape has no formula — but two roads reach it. SPLIT: cut into rectangles, add the pieces: $8 \times 4$ plus $5 \times 2$ gives $32 + 10 = 42$ m².
FILL AND SUBTRACT: restore the whole $8 \times 6$ ($48$), remove the $3 \times 2$ bite ($6$): $42$ m².
The roads MUST agree — and when they do, you've proof-read your own answer. Take both roads whenever the stakes are real.

examples.prompt: The $8 \times 6$ room with a $3 \times 2$ bite.
A $9 \times 7$ yard minus a $4 \times 3$ shed.

steps.title: Pick a road
steps.intro: Either works; agreement is the receipt.

problems.prompt: A $10 \times 8$ hall with a $4 \times 2$ alcove REMOVED has area:
problems.explanation: $80 - 8 = 72$ m². ($80$ forgot the alcove ever left.)

problems.prompt: An L-shape splits into $6 \times 3$ and $4 \times 2$ pieces. Its area is:
A U-shaped counter is a $12 \times 5$ slab with a $6 \times 3$ notch cut from one long side. Its area:

steps.title: The lazy rectangle
steps.prompt: A student answers the L-shape (an $8 \times 6$ with a $3 \times 2$ bite) as $48$ m². The slip:
options: the bite never left — $48$ is the FULL rectangle; the L holds $42$
areas of L-shapes cannot be found
steps.explanation: $8 \times 6$ measures the restored rectangle. The room is missing its bite: $48 - 6 = 42$ m² — or split it and see the same.

steps.title: Architects live in composite figures
steps.body: Almost no real floor plan is a single rectangle — kitchens notch into living rooms, closets bite corners. Architects compute floor areas exactly as you just did: split into rectangles, add, and cross-check by subtracting from the outline. Same two roads, drawn to scale.

steps.title: Missing edges, and keeping perimeter separate
beats: Composite figures hide some labels — but opposite spans must MATCH: if the whole top is $8$ and one bottom piece is $3$, the other is $8 - 3 = 5$.
Recover every edge before computing; each missing one is a difference of labelled ones.

And keep the two measures apart: cutting a bite from a rectangle REDUCES its area but (for a corner bite) the perimeter stays the same walk — the boundary just turns more corners. Area and perimeter move independently.

examples.prompt: Top edge $12$; lower-right piece spans $7$. The unlabelled span?
Corner bite of $3 \times 2$ from the $8 \times 6$: what happens to the perimeter?
steps: The bite's two new edges ($3$ and $2$) replace the two removed spans ($3$ and $2$) — the walk is unchanged: $2(8 + 6) = 28$ m.
Area fell to $42$; perimeter stayed $28$. The measures move independently.

problems.prompt: An L-shape's left side is $9$; the upper piece's height is $4$. The lower piece's height is:
problems.explanation: $9 - 4 = 5$ — heights along one side must add to the whole.

problems.prompt: An L-shape has whole width $7$; the labelled piece is $4$ wide. The unlabelled strip beside it is $6$ tall. The strip's area is:
problems.explanation: Strip width $7 - 4 = 3$; area $3 \times 6 = 18$.

problems.prompt: A corner bite is cut from a rectangle. Which changes?
options: the area only — the corner-bite walk keeps the same perimeter
problems.explanation: The bite's new edges exactly replace the removed spans, so the walk's length survives; the field, though, shrinks by the bite.

steps.title: Split without overlap
steps.prompt: Splitting an L into pieces that OVERLAP by a $2 \times 1$ patch makes the sum:
options: $2$ m² too big — the patch was counted twice
steps.explanation: Overlapping tiles get counted in both pieces: the sum overshoots by the overlap's area. Splits must tile the shape exactly — edge to edge, no sharing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Split-and-add or fill-and-subtract — take both roads; agreement is the receipt.
Missing edges are differences of labelled ones; recover them all first.
Splits must tile exactly — overlaps double-count.
A corner bite shrinks the area but leaves the perimeter's walk unchanged.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every figure below, travel BOTH roads (or check spans twice) before answering — the agreement habit is the whole lesson.

problems.explanation: $1\,200 - 600 = 600$ cm² of visible border.

problems.prompt: A staircase-shaped figure: steps of $2 \times 2$, $4 \times 2$ and $6 \times 2$ stacked. Total area:
problems.explanation: $4 + 8 + 12 = 24$ — three strips, no overlaps.

problems.prompt: A T-stage ($10 \times 3$ bar on a $4 \times 5$ stem) is painted with cans that each cover $50$ m². How many cans does one coat need?
options: $1$ can — the stage is exactly $50$ m²
problems.explanation: Bar $30$ + stem $20$ = $50$ m² — one can, to the brim.

steps.title: You've finished "Geometry — Shapes & Area" — the whole topic
steps.body: Angles, shape families, the boundary walk, the tile count, and figures built from pieces — with two-road receipts throughout. One topic remains in Grade 5: reading and drawing data.

practice.statement: On a straight line, three angles measure $40^\circ$, $90^\circ$ and one more. Find it.
A triangle has angles $48^\circ$ and $64^\circ$. Find the third and classify by angles.
practice.solution: $180 - 48 - 64 = 68^\circ$ — all three under $90$: an acute triangle.

practice.statement: A parallelogram has one angle of $75^\circ$. List all four angles.
Find the perimeter and area of a $16$ m by $9$ m sports court, with correct units.
A rectangle has perimeter $54$ cm and width $12$ cm. Find its length and its area.
Show that a $9 \times 3$ and a $6 \times 6$ rectangle share a perimeter but not an area.
practice.solution: Perimeters: $2(9+3) = 24$ and $2(6+6) = 24$ — equal. Areas: $27$ and $36$ m² — the square holds $9$ m² more.

practice.statement: An L-shaped patio is a $7 \times 6$ m rectangle with a $3 \times 2$ m bite. Find the area by both roads.
practice.solution: Subtract: $42 - 6 = 36$ m². Split: $7 \times 4 = 28$ plus $(7-3) \times 2 = 8$: $36$ m². Roads agree ✓.

practice.statement: A $12 \times 10$ m garden holds a $4 \times 4$ m pond. Grass covers the rest; how much?

testYourself.statement: Around a point sit angles of $110^\circ$, $85^\circ$, $75^\circ$ and one more. Find it and classify it.
An isosceles triangle has a $100^\circ$ angle at its top. Find the two base angles.
testYourself.solution: The base pair shares $180 - 100 = 80$ equally: $40^\circ$ each. Check: $100 + 40 + 40 = 180$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: Which of these can NOT be a triangle's angles: $(60, 60, 60)$, $(90, 45, 45)$, $(100, 50, 40)$? Why?
testYourself.solution: $100 + 50 + 40 = 190 \ne 180$ — the third set overspends the budget. The others close exactly.

testYourself.statement: A square courtyard takes $60$ m of fencing. Find its side and its area.
A room is $11$ m by $4$ m. Give its area and perimeter — and name which one carpet needs and which one skirting board needs.
testYourself.solution: Area $44$ m² (carpet); perimeter $2(11 + 4) = 30$ m (skirting). Tiles inside, walk around.

testYourself.statement: A T-shaped stage is a $12 \times 4$ m bar atop a $6 \times 5$ m stem. Find its area by splitting, and check by surrounding it with a $12 \times 9$ rectangle and subtracting the two shoulders.
testYourself.solution: Split: $48 + 30 = 78$ m². Surround: $12 \times 9 = 108$, shoulders $2 \times (3 \times 5) = 30$: $108 - 30 = 78$ m² — roads agree ✓.
